items.prose: After twenty-one days of continuous gravity flow, a gelatinous biological skin (schmutzdecke) matured across the quartz sand bed. Protozoa and sessile bacteria in the zoogleal biofilm digested suspended organic matter, dropping turbidity from 14.5 NTU to 0.25 NTU.

Accumulated silt and diatom carcasses increased hydraulic head loss to 1.8 meters, choking filtration to 0.05 m/hr. Workers drained the bed and scraped off the top 15mm of clogged sand; upon re-submersion, flow restored to design capacity within six hours.

Sieve gradation of the river quartz sand confirmed an effective size (d10) of 0.28mm and a uniformity coefficient (Cu) of 1.95. The narrow grain size distribution prevented fine sand migration while sustaining laminar interstitial percolation.

Fluorescence microscopy confirmed 99.98% physical entrapment of 4-micron *Cryptosporidium* oocysts within the top 30mm of the biological sand matrix. The sticky extracellular polysaccharides produced by the bacterial flora prevented parasite breakthrough.

Filtered water collected through slotted vitrified clay tiles beneath a four-layer graded gravel support bed. The uniform drainage grid maintained balanced drawdown across 200 square meters of bed area without localized funneling or sand piping.

Subterranean intake water chilled to 2.5°C during the winter cold snap, depressing bacterial metabolic rates by 60%. Pathogen digestion efficiency collapsed, requiring operators to throttle flow to 0.08 m/hr and supplement with auxiliary UV disinfection.

Pumping cold, oxygen-saturated well water into a warmer sand basin released dissolved gas bubbles inside the sand pores. This 'air binding' phenomenon choked interstitial pathways, causing a false head loss surge and stopping water flow completely.

After years of scrapings reduced bed depth to 50cm, operators used the wet-trenching technique to add 40cm of fresh sand underneath the existing biological layer. Burying the active biofilm on top of new sand preserved the living culture with zero ripening lag.
